figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Knowledge-latency motivation and shared persona context. Behavior may change before the next detector release. Offline-refreshed entity, group, and interaction records supply shared context to detector-specific adapters, which combine this context with each detector’s own score, while the four detectors remain frozen. Detectors 1–4 are Visa’s proprietary detection models: one production and three internal.A two-part schematic. The left panel contrasts entity behavior changing over weeks with a months-long detector release cycle. The right panel shows an offline-refreshed shared persona memory feeding four detector-specific adapters, each of which also receives a score from its corresponding frozen detector.
figures.headline: Offline-refreshed shared persona memory feeds four frozen detectors through adapters, so behavior updates need no detector release.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: PersonaAgent lifecycle. (A) Three LLM proposal roles and a Protocol Critic perform bounded protocol self-evolution. A prespecified rule selects revisions using development-set results. (B) Weekly refresh updates numerical persona memory under the frozen protocol and fixed topic definitions. (C) Exact-key lookup and predefined fallback supply one record for each of five views. The adapter combines these with the frozen base score and its metadata-adjusted version. LLMs are used only at design time. A three-stage workflow. Offline construction contains a role-based protocol-design loop and a weekly refresh for five persona views. Online scoring produces one matched or fallback record per view, using fixed missing-value indicators when neither is available, and combines their numerical feature vector with the frozen detector's base score and predefined transaction metadata through a lightweight adapter to produce the final score.
figures.headline: Offline protocol design and weekly refresh feed online scoring, where one record per view and the frozen base score combine in a lightweight adapter.
citing_sentences: PersonaAgent has three core parts, one for each stage in Fig. 2: agentic persona-protocol self-evolution, Semantic Persona Memory, and a tree-based adapter for each detector.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Release control and request serving. Memory, release metadata, and compatible adapters are activated atomically as one package only after build and compatibility checks pass. Each scoring request selects one package version by event time and detector; health monitoring can halt a rollout or restore the complete previous package. If package selection or serving fails, the frozen base score is returned. A two-part system diagram. Release control validates a candidate package, activates it as a unit on success, and retains the active package on rejection. A previous complete package is retained for rollback. Each request pins a compatible package using event time and detector identity before serving. Sparse or unseen keys use predefined fallback records and continue scoring; pinning or serving failures instead return the frozen base score. Lookup, latency, and score-shift monitoring feeds back to release control.

abstract: In large-scale payment networks, entities (card, merchant, etc.) and their interactions play a key role in transaction anomaly detection. However, transaction patterns between different entities usually change more frequently than the production model refresh schedule. Meanwhile, entity embedding tables suffer from high-cardinality and sparse interaction issues. To resolve the above challenges, we present PersonaAgent, an agentic transaction anomaly detection framework which represents the latest entity behavior signals as personas and saves them in a refreshable memory. Offline, a weekly scheduled batch job is used to extract the latest behavior signals and update them in the memory. At inference time, a lightweight adapter retrieves the corresponding entity behavior signals of each transaction from memory and uses them to augment the base anomaly classifier’s scoring. Through comprehensive benchmarking with different anomaly detection models at Visa, PersonaAgent is able to score transactions efficiently (a 1,000-transaction CPU batch in 1–2 ms), lifting the PR-AUC by 0.65–6.58% and the production business metric by 8.93–14.24% relatively in deployment.

sections.body: The paper names a knowledge-latency gap: entity behavior can be re-estimated weekly, while a detector's update cycle typically lasts at least several months. PersonaAgent stores multi-entity behavior records in Semantic Persona Memory, refreshed weekly without changing detector weights. LLM agents act only at design time to propose a persona protocol. At scoring time, a lightweight, tree-based adapter for each frozen detector combines five persona-view records with the base score. In deployment, the production business metric (BM1) improved by a relative 8.93–14.24% across four detectors.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Entity behavior changes faster than detector releases, so the paper stores behavior in refreshable persona memory outside frozen detectors.

sections.body: The section groups related work into three areas: transaction representations, such as foundation models, sequential tabular transformers, and entity embedding tables; retrieval-augmented scoring, including tabular nearest-neighbor methods and BRIGHT; and LLM-based optimizers, such as CAAFE and FeatLLM. The text states three differences for PersonaAgent. It serves records by deterministic key lookup with predefined fallback, so online scoring needs no similarity search or generation. It releases memory and compatible adapters as one versioned package. It accepts a protocol revision only when development BM1 improves and the required checks pass.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work spans transaction models, retrieval-augmented scoring, and agentic optimization, and PersonaAgent differs by keeping language models offline.

sections.body: A transaction's outcome may arrive much later, so each memory snapshot uses only outcomes available by its cutoff T. A transaction is scored with the release package active at its event time. Each detector is a frozen black-box function that returns a base score between 0 and 1. The adapter combines that base score, the persona records, and a metadata input into a final score. The metrics are BM1, PR-AUC and AUC, where higher is better. Because the absolute values are confidential, each is reported as a relative improvement over the frozen base, so +10% means 1.1 times the base value.
sections.heading: Preliminaries and Problem Formulation
sections.headline: Adapters must use only evidence available by each memory cutoff, while detectors stay frozen and metrics are relative to the base.

sections.body: The method has three parts. First, LLM roles propose changes to a persona protocol with five parts: behavior signals, narrative schema, topic construction, retrieval rules, and release checks. A Protocol Critic diagnoses each candidate, and a prespecified rule selects the protocol to freeze using development BM1. Second, each weekly batch applies the frozen protocol to cutoff-valid history and builds a memory snapshot. The snapshot is activated only after validation, together with compatible adapters. Third, each adapter reads five numerical records and the frozen base score to compute the final score. Scoring is deterministic and calls no LLM.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: A design-time agent search builds a persona protocol, a weekly batch refreshes memory, and per-detector adapters score transactions deterministically.

sections.body: Each detector's final score is compared with its own frozen base score on the same metrics. For RQ1, all 24 detector, period and metric comparisons show improvements, and each 95% confidence interval lies above zero from a paired bootstrap over transactions. Deployment gains were 8.93–14.24% in BM1, 0.65–6.58% in PR-AUC and 0.23–0.66% in AUC. Relative improvements fall from Period 1 to Period 2 in eight of twelve detector and metric combinations. Matched ablations credit the five persona views with average gains of 3.20 and 0.44 percentage points in PR-AUC and AUC over the variant without them.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: PersonaAgent improved all four frozen detectors on every metric in both the held-out test and live deployment.

sections.body: Topic identity counts as part of compatibility. If a topic ID were reused for different behavior, the adapter would still accept its inputs and misread them, so topic identity is checked alongside schema and fallback. The validated release package is the unit of activation, maintenance and rollback. The record-age test found the BM1 relative improvement lower for every detector when topic and interaction records come from the preceding weekly build. The section proposes comparing weekly refresh with a fixed package. It also warns that Location-derived signals may correlate with sensitive attributes, so subgroup-impact assessment should precede policy-level use.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Stable topic identities and versioned packages let entity knowledge update without detector releases, though gains shrink with older records.

sections.body: The paper addresses the gap between weekly re-estimation of entity behavior and detector release cycles that last months. Behavior is kept in a shared, refreshable persona memory outside the detectors. Semantic topics pool evidence for rare and cold-start entities. A bounded agentic search at design time selects the protocol, and online scoring uses deterministic retrieval and adapters with no LLM calls. One release package, unchanged across both periods, improved every reported metric for four detectors offline and in deployment, where BM1 rose by a relative 8.93–14.24%.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: One validated release package improved four detectors offline and in deployment, with business metric gains of 8.93–14.24% relative.

sections.body: The privacy statement says the paper withholds account numbers, raw merchant names, Location identities, detector identity and absolute performance values. The appendix also gives deployment controls and failure handling (Table 5), persona-record fields (Table 6), memory construction, retrieval keys and fallback rules. It includes a worked protocol example and the design, refresh and serving algorithms (Algorithms 1–3). Supplementary diagnostics cover bootstrap and seed-refit details, cross-period and record-age tests, matched-ablation settings, and the correction-fingerprint definition.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists privacy and compliance terms, deployment controls, persona record fields, fallback rules, search algorithms, and supplementary diagnostics.
